choices.term: εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἔστιν ἐν σαρκί ... ἀλλ' οὖν ὑπὲρ σάρκα νοεῖται
choices.english: even though He is in the flesh ... yet He is understood to be above the flesh
choices.why: The risen Christ keeps His flesh yet is above its weakness.
rejected: though he lived a human life

choices.term: ὁ τοῦ θανάτου πατήσας τὸ κράτος
choices.english: He who trampled the might of death
rejected: He who once brought death into power

choices.english: All these, he says, have passed away
rejected: we are to regard all these things as passed away

choices.term: οὐκ ἀβούλητον τῷ Πατρὶ τῆς μετὰ σαρκὸς οἰκονομίας τὸ μυστήριον καὶ ἡ δι' αὐτοῦ καινουργία
choices.english: the mystery of the economy in the flesh, and the renewal made through Him, are not against the Father's will
choices.why: Both nouns are subjects of one litotes; 'pleasing' would add a claim.

choices.term: ἐκπεπολεμωμένους αὐτῷ διὰ τῆς εἰς πολύθεον πλάνης ἕλληνας, καὶ ἰουδαίους διά γε τοῦ βούλεσθαι ταῖς κατὰ νόμον προσπεπῆχθαι σκιαῖς
choices.english: Greeks, who had been made His enemies by straying into the worship of many gods, and Jews, by wishing to stay fastened to the shadows of the law
choices.why: ἐκπολεμόω governs both groups; προσπήγνυμι, to fasten to.
rejected: Greeks lost in much-god delusion, Jews fallen upon the shadows

choices.term: Θεὸν οὖν ἄρα καὶ ἰσοκλεᾶ τῷ Πατρὶ διακηρύττουσιν αὐτόν
choices.english: they proclaim Him God, equal in glory to the Father
choices.why: Christ gave the ministry, yet Paul calls the giver God; so Christ is God.

choices.term: ὀρέγει δὲ πάλιν ἐπ' ἐξουσίᾳ ὡς Θεὸς ὁ Υἱός
choices.english: the Son in turn, as God, extends it with authority
choices.why: The Son is the subject; the Father grants and the Son bestows.
rejected: God grants it as both God and Father

choices.english: to the sacred service of the gospel's decrees

choices.term: οἷον αὐτοῦ τὸ πρόσωπον ἀναλαβόντες Χριστοῦ
choices.english: taking up as it were the very person of Christ
choices.why: πρόσωπον here as 'person' or 'role': the apostles speak in Christ's stead (2 Corinthians 5:20).
rejected: taking up as it were his face Christ

pass_a_gloss: [opens inside the quotation begun in the previous section: 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among'] us', and he underwent (ὑφίστημι, aor.) the death on behalf of the life of all [col. 353] according to flesh, and thus we have known (γινώσκω, pf.) him; but from now we know [him] no longer; for even if he is also in flesh, for on the third day (τριήμερος) he came back to life (ἀναβιόω) and is with the Father in the heavens, yet he is understood (νοέω, pass.) above (ὑπέρ) flesh; for having died once (ἅπαξ) 'he no longer dies, death no longer is lord over (κυριεύω) him; for what he died, he died to sin once for all (ἐφάπαξ); but what he lives, he lives to God.' So if the author (ἀρχηγός) of our life has come to be in these [things], [it is] in every way a necessity that we ourselves too, having followed closely (κατακολουθέω) his footprints (ἴχνος), be understood not rather in flesh, but above flesh. Very rightly, then, the inspired (θεσπέσιος) Paul. 'So if anyone [is] in Christ, a new creation (κτίσις)', he says; 'the ancient (ἀρχαῖος) things passed away (παρέρχομαι); see, new things have come to be.' For ancient [is] the 'Earth you are and into earth you will go away (ἀπέρχομαι)'; and indeed also that in the book (βίβλος) of Moses: 'For the mind (διάνοια) of man is intently (ἐπιμελῶς) set upon (ἔγκειμαι) the evil things from youth (νεότης)'; and ancient besides these also the things in the law; all these indeed he says have passed by (παρελαύνω); for we have been justified (δικαιόω, pf. pass.) through faith in Christ, and the power of the curse (ἀρά) has ceased (παύω, pf. pass.); for the one who trampled (πατέω) the might (κράτος) of death came back to life on our behalf, and we have known the one being God by nature and truly, fulfilling (πληρόω) the worship (λατρεία) in spirit and truth, the Son mediating (μεσιτεύω) and giving the blessings (εὐλογία) from above and from the Father to the world; whence also very wisely the inspired Paul says: 'And all things [are] from God, who reconciled (καταλλάσσω) us to himself through Christ.' For truly the mystery of the economy (οἰκονομία) with flesh, and the renewal (καινουργία) through him, is not unwilled (ἀβούλητος) by the Father. And the initiator (μυσταγωγός) adds to these that the Father himself reconciled us to himself through Christ, Greeks made enemies to him (ἐκπολεμόω, pf. pass.) through the [col. 354] wandering (πλάνη) into many gods (πολύθεος), and Jews through wishing to have been fastened (προσπήγνυμι, pf. pass.) to the shadows (σκιά) according to the law and not to admit (προσίημι, mid.) the word of the true worship; for through him we have had (ἔχω, pf.) the access (προσαγωγή), and 'No one comes to the Father', as he himself says, 'except through' him. So 'all things [are] from the God who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry (διακονία) of the reconciliation (καταλλαγή).' Observe (ἀθρέω) for me again that, Christ having given them the ministry of reconciliation, for they have been appointed (χειροτονέω, pf. pass.) through him to apostleship, he said God [was] the one who gave; God therefore and equal in glory (ἰσοκλεής) to the Father they proclaim (διακηρύσσω) him, knowing one lordship (κυριότης) and authority (ἐξουσία) of both; of what sort then is it, what is this word upon the ministry, or what the manner of the reconciliation, he brings on (ἐπιφέρω) saying: 'God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself', that is, the one in Christ reconciling the world to himself was God; for through faith, as I said, in Christ, we have made peace (εἰρηνεύω) toward God, or we have been reconciled (καταλλάσσω, pf. pass.). And of this a clear proof (ἀπόδειξις) [is] the forgiveness (ἄφεσις) of the offences (πλημμελέω, pf. pass. ptc.), which the God and Father grants (χαρίζομαι); and the Son in turn holds [it] out (ὀρέγω) with authority as God, saying to the paralytic (παραλυτικός): 'Your sins are forgiven (ἀφίημι, pf. pass.) you.' So in Christ, that is, in the person (πρόσωπον) of Christ, God reconciles the world to himself, not reckoning (λογίζομαι) [col. 355] to those who have sinned their trespasses (παράπτωμα). And since we have been appointed (τάσσω, pf. pass.), he says, to the sacred service (ἱερουργία) of the gospel decrees (θέσπισμα), and the word of the reconciliation has been placed (τίθημι, pf. pass.) in us, for we are ministers of God, necessarily [we make] for those having thus believed (πιστεύω, pf.) the entreaties (λιτή) on behalf of themselves (the clause has no verb), and as it were taking up (ἀναλαμβάνω) the very person of Christ, we say to those wishing to drift away (ἀποφοιτάω): 'We beg (δέομαι) on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God', believing into him, plainly the one on whose behalf we are ambassadors (πρεσβεύω); [stray numeral 14 omitted] for Christ [is] the door (θύρα) and he himself the way (ὁδός). And since it was likely that some would disregard (ἀλογέω) the gospel preachings (κήρυγμα), and reckon as nothing the truly acceptable (εὐπρόσδεκτος) time of salvation (σωτηρία), and after this thrust aside (παρωθέω) the faith, the initiator further devises (προσεπινοέω) something for them again, holding not unable (οὐκ ἀνικάνως) toward shame (ἐντροπή), and toward persuading (ἀναπείθω) [them] easily not to [cut off; the sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … us” (John 1:14), and He underwent death in the flesh for the life of all, and so we have known Him; but from now on we know Him so no longer. For even though He is in the flesh, since He came back to life on the third day and is with the Father in heaven, yet He is understood to be above the flesh. For having died once, He “dies no more; death no longer has dominion over Him. For the death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10). If, then, the Author of our life (Acts 3:15) has come to be in this state, it is altogether necessary that we too, following in His footsteps (1 Peter 2:21), be understood to be not in the flesh but rather above the flesh. Very rightly, then, does the inspired Paul speak.
“So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,” he says; “the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

For the old is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19), and also that word in the book of Moses, “For the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). Old as well, besides these, are the things in the law. All these, he says, have passed away; for we have been justified through faith in Christ, and the power of the curse has ceased. He who trampled the might of death came back to life for us, and we have come to know Him who is God by nature and in truth, as we fulfil the worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:23–24), while the Son mediates and gives the world the blessings from above and from the Father. Hence the inspired Paul says very wisely: “All things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:18). For truly, the mystery of the economy in the flesh, and the renewal made through Him, are not against the Father’s will.

Our guide into the mysteries adds to this that the Father Himself reconciled us to Himself through Christ: us Greeks, who had been made His enemies by straying into the worship of many gods, and Jews, by wishing to stay fastened to the shadows of the law and not accepting the message of true worship. For through Him we have obtained access (Ephesians 2:18), and “no one comes to the Father,” as He Himself says, “except through” Him (John 14:6). So “all things are from God, who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Notice again, I ask you, that although it was Christ who gave them the ministry of reconciliation, for they were appointed to apostleship through Him, he said that God was the giver. So they proclaim Him God, equal in glory to the Father, knowing that the two have one lordship and authority. What sort, then, is this word concerning the ministry, or what is the manner of the reconciliation? He goes on to say: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19), that is, He who was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ was God. For through faith in Christ, as I said, we have made peace with God (Romans 5:1), that is, we have been reconciled. And a clear proof of this is the forgiveness of our offences, which the God and Father grants; and the Son in turn, as God, extends it with authority, saying to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2; Luke 5:20). So “in Christ,” that is, in the person of Christ, God reconciles the world to Himself, “not counting” their trespasses against those who have sinned (2 Corinthians 5:19).

Since, he says, we have been appointed to the sacred service of the gospel’s decrees, and the word of reconciliation has been placed in us (2 Corinthians 5:19), for we are God’s ministers (2 Corinthians 6:4), we must make entreaties to those who have believed in this way, for their own sake; and, taking up as it were the very person of Christ, we say to those who wish to drift away: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20), by believing in Him, that is, clearly, in the One on whose behalf we are ambassadors. For Christ is the door (John 10:9), and He Himself is the way (John 14:6).

But since it was likely that some would disregard the gospel preaching, count as nothing the truly “acceptable time” of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and after this thrust the faith aside, our guide into the mysteries devises something more for them, well able to shame them and to persuade them readily not to …
